sheet: Critical number: f′(c)=0 or f′ undefined, with f(c) defined.
Fermat: differentiable interior local extremum ⇒ f′(c)=0.
No derivative sign change ⇒ neither by first derivative test.
f′(c)=0 and f′′(c)>0 ⇒ strict local minimum.
f′(c)=0 and f′′(c)<0 ⇒ strict local maximum.

cards: Check endpoints and all interior candidates
tricks: Factor f′ before making a sign chart.
Test one value in each interval separated by critical numbers.
Do not call every stationary point an extremum.

For absolute extrema, never omit endpoints.
shortcuts: x² at zero: minimum; −x²: maximum; x³: neither; x⁴: minimum.
For x³−3x, stationary points are −1 and 1.
Closed interval global extrema require a finite candidate comparison.

howto: Use a fixed sequence: find critical numbers, classify each with derivative signs or the second derivative test, then compare endpoints if the question asks for absolute extrema. Keep local and global language distinct.

scenes.title: Foundation: derivatives and critical points
scenes.objective: Recall how derivatives identify candidate extrema.

ask.q: What does f′(x)>0 on an interval mean?
ask.nudge: It describes the direction of change.

body: The derivative is the instantaneous slope. A positive derivative means increasing; a negative derivative means decreasing.
A turning point is usually associated with a derivative sign change. But f′(c)=0 alone does not prove a maximum or minimum: x³ has a stationary point at zero and keeps increasing.

items.recall: An interior point where f′(c)=0 or f′ does not exist, with f(c) defined.
refresh: Critical numbers are candidates, not guaranteed extrema. A cusp such as |x| can be an extremum even though the derivative does not exist.
For absolute extrema on a closed interval, include endpoints as well as interior critical numbers. The endpoint values may be the global maximum or minimum.

items.ask: What sign change gives a local maximum?
items.recall: f′ changes from positive to negative.
refresh: Positive derivative means the function rises; negative derivative means it falls. Rising then falling produces a local peak.
If the sign stays the same on both sides, the first derivative test does not give an extremum. For x³, f′=3x² is non-negative on both sides of zero.

items.ask: What does f′′(c)>0 imply when f′(c)=0?
items.recall: A strict local minimum, by the second derivative test.
refresh: A positive second derivative indicates local concavity upward. At a stationary point, this produces a strict local minimum; a negative second derivative gives a strict local maximum.
When f′′(c)=0, the test is inconclusive. x⁴ has a minimum at zero, while x³ has neither a maximum nor minimum there.

scenes.title: Turning points are changes of direction
scenes.objective: Connect derivative signs with graph behaviour.

ask.q: For f(x)=x² at zero, how does f′ change sign?
ask.nudge: f′=2x is negative before zero and positive after.

body: A local maximum is a rise followed by a fall. A local minimum is a fall followed by a rise.
A stationary point only means the tangent is horizontal. It may be a stationary inflection, so always check what happens on both sides.

scenes.title: Local and absolute extrema
scenes.objective: Distinguish neighbourhood comparisons from global comparisons.

ask.q: Can a local minimum fail to be the absolute minimum?
ask.nudge: Another valley elsewhere may be lower.

blocks.body: A local maximum at c means f(c)≥f(x) for all x sufficiently close to c. A local minimum reverses the inequality.
An absolute maximum or minimum compares f(c) with every point in the domain, not merely nearby points.
A continuous function on a closed and bounded interval [a,b] attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum.

scenes.title: Fermat's theorem and candidate points
scenes.objective: Use the necessary condition without treating it as sufficient.

ask.q: At a differentiable interior local extremum, what must f′(c) be?
ask.nudge: A smooth peak or trough has a horizontal tangent.

blocks.body: If f has a local maximum or minimum at an interior point c and is differentiable there, then f′(c)=0.
Solve f′(x)=0 and include interior points where f′ is undefined but f is defined. On a closed interval, add both endpoints.
Fermat's theorem identifies candidates only. A stationary point may be neither a maximum nor a minimum; use derivative signs or a sufficient second-derivative condition.

scenes.title: Worked: classify x³−3x
scenes.objective: Use derivative signs to identify local extrema.

ask.q: For f(x)=x³−3x, which stationary point is the local maximum?
ask.nudge: The derivative changes + to − at x=−1.

scenes.problem: Find and classify stationary points of f(x)=x³−3x.

steps.why: The function changes from increasing to decreasing at −1 and decreasing to increasing at 1.
There is a local maximum 2 at −1 and a local minimum −2 at 1.

scenario.teaser: A cost curve has a best operating point.
scenario.title: Local optima in a production-cost curve
body: A cost curve may rise, fall and rise again as output changes. A stationary point is a candidate operating level, but the derivative sign determines whether it is a local cost minimum or maximum.
If marginal cost changes from negative to positive, total cost has a local minimum. If it changes from positive to negative, total cost has a local maximum.
A local minimum need not be the absolute minimum over the feasible output range. Operational constraints create endpoints, and those must be compared when the question asks for a global optimum.

scenes.title: The first derivative test
scenes.objective: Classify critical points with a sign chart.

ask.q: If f′ is negative on both sides of c, is c a local extremum?
ask.nudge: The function is decreasing on both sides.

blocks.body: f′: + to − gives a local maximum. f′: − to + gives a local minimum. No sign change gives neither by this test.
Factor f′, mark its zeros and undefined points, then test one value in each interval. The sign chart is more reliable than guessing from a sketch.
For x³, f′(0)=0 but f′ remains positive on either side. The function keeps increasing, so zero is not a local extremum.

scenes.title: Guided: second derivative test
scenes.objective: Use concavity at a stationary point.
scenes.problem: Classify the stationary point of f(x)=x²−4x+7.
hints: The stationary point is x=2. Now compute f′′.
f′′=2>0, so the graph is concave upward.
scenes.answer: Strict local minimum at x=2, with value 3.
scenes.solution: f′=2x−4=0 gives x=2. Since f′′=2>0, the second derivative test gives a strict local minimum. Substitution gives f(2)=4−8+7=3.

ask.nudge: The second derivative test is inconclusive.

scenes.title: Second derivative test and its limits
scenes.objective: Know when the concavity shortcut is conclusive.

ask.q: For x⁴ at zero, f′′(0)=0. Is zero still a minimum?
ask.nudge: Use the sign of x⁴ or the first derivative test.

blocks.body: If f′(c)=0 and f′′(c)>0, c is a strict local minimum. If f′′(c)<0, c is a strict local maximum.
If f′′(c)=0, no conclusion follows. x⁴ has a minimum at zero, while x³ has neither a maximum nor a minimum.
Check the sign of f′ on both sides, compare nearby values, or use higher-order analysis when justified.

scenes.title: Guided: absolute extrema on [−2,2]
scenes.objective: Compare endpoints with all interior candidates.
scenes.problem: Find the absolute maximum and minimum of f(x)=x³−3x on [−2,2].
hints: Solve f′(x)=3x²−3=0 to find interior critical numbers.
Compare all four values, not just the stationary values.
scenes.answer: Absolute maximum 2 at −1 and 2; absolute minimum −2 at −2 and 1.
scenes.solution: Critical numbers are −1 and 1. Values are f(−2)=−2, f(−1)=2, f(1)=−2 and f(2)=2. The absolute maximum is 2 and the absolute minimum is −2.

ask.q: Why must both endpoints be checked?
ask.nudge: An absolute extremum can occur at the boundary.

scenes.title: Local does not mean global

ask.q: How do you find the absolute minimum on [a,b] when there are two local minima?
ask.nudge: Compare both local minima and the endpoints.

body: A local minimum is only the lowest point in a small neighbourhood. Another valley elsewhere may be lower, and an endpoint may be lower still.
On a closed interval, find every interior critical candidate, evaluate the function at each, evaluate both endpoints, and compare all values.

scenario.teaser: A design variable is constrained to a feasible interval.
scenario.title: Comparing local and global engineering optima
body: A design objective may have several stationary points inside a feasible range. One may be a local minimum but still have a larger objective value than a boundary design.

For a continuous objective on a closed bounded feasible interval, the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees global extrema. The calculation must compare every interior critical candidate with both endpoints.
This distinction matters in optimisation: a calculus stationary point is not automatically the best feasible design. Constraints can make a boundary point globally optimal.

scenes.objective: Contrast x⁴ and x³ at zero.

ask.q: Both x⁴ and x³ have f′′(0)=0. Do they have the same classification?
ask.nudge: Compare the sign of the first derivative.

scenes.problem: Classify x⁴ and x³ at x=0.

steps.why: The derivative changes from negative to positive, so zero is a strict minimum.
The derivative remains positive on both sides, so zero is not an extremum.
A zero second derivative is inconclusive, not a classification.

scenes.title: Trap check: six statements
scenes.intro: Judge each statement true or false.

items.claim: Every differentiable interior local extremum has derivative zero.
items.why: Fermat's theorem gives this necessary condition.

items.claim: Every stationary point is a local extremum.
items.why: x³ has a stationary inflection at zero.

items.claim: A positive second derivative at a stationary point gives a local minimum.
items.why: The graph is locally concave upward.

items.claim: If the second derivative is zero, there is no extremum.
items.why: x⁴ has a minimum at zero despite f′′(0)=0.

items.claim: Absolute extrema on a closed interval may occur at endpoints.
items.why: Endpoints are part of the domain and must be checked.

items.claim: The Extreme Value Theorem applies to every continuous function on an open interval.
items.why: The standard theorem requires a closed and bounded interval.

scenes.title: Final optimisation checklist
body: 1. Find critical numbers: f′=0 or f′ undefined, with f defined.
2. First derivative test: + to − maximum; − to + minimum; no change means neither.
3. At a stationary point, f′′>0 gives a local minimum; f′′<0 gives a local maximum.
4. If f′′=0, use a sign chart or another method; the test is inconclusive.
5. For absolute extrema on [a,b], evaluate all interior critical candidates and both endpoints.
6. A continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains absolute maximum and minimum.
